expl: Fact 1 says even arbitrary labels can create an in-group comparison frame. The deep-history answer misses how thin the trigger can be.
Fact 2 says perceived membership can alter empathy. Competition may sharpen the effect, but equal concern is not the default guarantee.
Fact 3 supports the dehumanization answer. The error is thinking violence needs personal hatred before ideology lowers concern.
Fact 4 says racial categories are culturally learned. The fixed-taxonomy answer treats social meaning as if it were biology alone.
Fact 5 points to superordinate goals. Contact works best when conditions make cooperation necessary, not when rivals merely share space.
Fact 6 says rapid category responses can be regulated by later frontal processing. The claim mistakes a first spark for a final order.
Fact 7 says in-group loyalty can support generosity. The stronger reading keeps both sides: cooperation inside and danger outside.
Fact 8 says threat narratives increase punitive support. Fear can change what feels necessary, not just add facts to a policy ledger.
Fact 9 says cross-cutting identities weaken simple splits. The single-identity answer misses how one person can share and differ at once.
Fact 8 warns against reading startup friction as failure. The distractors expect instant ease or reduce the choice to price.
Fact 1 says a written list increases control, but the control has to serve the harder priority. An equal-weight list can still let easy work lead.
Fact 2 supports planning before work because it reduces decision friction. Waiting for interruptions makes the day's first pressure too powerful.
Fact 3 says longer planning horizons feed the daily list. The fix is not a bigger daily page; it is separating timing before choosing today's actions.
Fact 4 says priority marks convert a list into a sequence. The number of items matters less than whether the page tells work what comes first.
Fact 5 says unwritten tasks keep pulling attention. Writing them down frees the mind to compare and rank them instead of rehearsing them.
Fact 6 says a plan can be revised without being abandoned. A changed call asks for a changed page, not a surrender to drift.
Fact 7 says the daily list should be prepared before execution pressure peaks. Once replies and calls lead, planning starts behind the day.
Fact 8 says project planning benefits from listing every step first. The visible step can be tempting, but it may hide the real order.
Fact 9 says working from a list makes completion measurable. Feeling busy can mislead; the list shows whether the chosen work moved.
Fact 1 says skill gaps can cause procrastination. Easy work may feel active, but it can hide the skill friction inside the report.
Fact 2 supports improving the key skill first. Waiting for confidence reverses the order; practice is what helps confidence grow.
Fact 3 says learning should target tasks with high consequence. Interesting learning is a near miss when the delayed report needs a report skill.
Fact 4 says daily learning compounds over time. The trap is treating occasional learning as equal to repeated work on the same skill.
Fact 5 says feedback speeds skill improvement. More solo effort can repeat the same weak move if no one points out what is unclear.
Fact 6 says a weak skill should be named rather than hidden behind busyness. Easier work can keep motion alive while the gap stays untouched.
Fact 7 says training is productive when it supports execution. Course buying is a near miss if no real draft or practice follows.
Fact 8 says better skill lowers emotional resistance. The feeling does not automatically prove the task is wrong; it may point to the weak move.
Fact 9 says key-skill upgrading can multiply output. The near miss is assuming only tools or delegation can do that.
Fact 1 says large tasks should be divided into small pieces. The waiting choice treats size as a reason not to touch the proposal.
Fact 2 supports the small start. Waiting for the feeling to change keeps the report untouched.
Fact 3 says the Swiss cheese method uses partial work to weaken avoidance. The blanks can look messy, but the task has been entered.
Fact 4 says salami slices use sequential small completion. Opening everything can look active while no slice gets finished.
Fact 5 says a timed start separates beginning from finishing. Calling it fake work misses the value of getting the task open.
Fact 6 says momentum often appears after contact. The near miss is waiting for momentum before the first sentence.
Fact 7 says the first slice should be easy to identify. Broad wording can hide the next move even when it sounds responsible.
Fact 8 says slicing is not an excuse to avoid the whole result. Formatting checks are a near miss when the recommendation stays blank.
Fact 9 says small pieces need connection to the larger outcome. Finished bits can still miss if they do not move the report.
Fact 1 says complex work benefits from uninterrupted blocks. Spare gaps repeat the error that important work can always fit between other demands.
Fact 2 says high-value tasks require calendar protection. A margin note is a near miss because it names importance without reserving time.
Fact 3 says short fragments may be too small for deep progress. Adding up minutes misses the reentry cost of the report.
Fact 4 says early blocks can protect work from later interruption. Waiting for routine demands lets those demands claim the day first.
Fact 5 says setup costs make repeated reentry expensive. Review can sound useful, but here the repeated setup eats the time.
Fact 6 says a block should be tied to a specific outcome. A broad label can hide vagueness even when it sounds important.
Fact 7 says other people need to know when a block is protected. Silence leaves reasonable teammates guessing that she is available.
Fact 8 says large blocks are created, not found. Waiting for minor work to clear gives small tasks first claim on the calendar.
Fact 9 says the best block should go to the highest-consequence task. Ease and readiness are tempting but weaker sorting rules.
Fact 1 supports the timing claim: emotion prepares action before full explanation. The near misses treat feeling as late commentary or mere noise.
Fact 5 draws the line: usefulness does not guarantee accuracy. The wrong moves either obey every impulse or discard emotion outright.
Fact 1 supports the timing claim: the amygdala can start alarm before detailed cortical checking. The other choices make thought first or treat intensity as proof.
Fact 2 says the thalamus can route rough input in parallel. The neat-stream view misses how the body can ready itself before a full explanation lands.
Fact 3 explains disproportion: the cue becomes an emergency before context is checked. Treating intensity as accuracy is the exact trap.
Fact 4 says emotional memory stores feeling significance as well as details. A clear factual memory can still carry old threat or shame into the present.
Fact 5 supports the checking role of the prefrontal cortex. The willpower choice sounds firm but misses the timing and inhibition mechanism.
Fact 6 connects past trauma or humiliation with a lower threshold now. That explains the speed without declaring today's cue fully accurate.
Fact 7 keeps both sides in view: fast emotion can produce heroic speed or destructive action. The other choices make speed all bad or all wise.
Fact 8 says naming the mechanism can create a gap. It is not an excuse or proof of safety; it is a pause before conduct.
Fact 9 says emotional intelligence begins by seeing that the first impulse may be a false alarm. Intensity alone is not truth.
Fact 1 says IQ predicts some academic outcomes, not all life conduct. The grade-only view misses how emotion shifts attention, memory, and action.
Fact 2 ties impulse control to using ability under provocation. The near-miss says ability is separate, but the surge can steer it.
Fact 3 defines interpersonal intelligence as reading other people. Charm can help, but it is too thin to carry the whole skill.
Fact 4 says self-knowledge gives access to feelings and uses them as guidance. It is not self-absorption or a license to strike.
Fact 5 says emotional intelligence is a cluster of abilities. Friendliness is a tempting shortcut, but it hides the separate skills.
Fact 6 allows brilliance and bad choice to coexist. The error is assuming smart people cannot self-sabotage under emotional pressure.
Fact 7 warns that cognitive rewards alone can miss adult capacities. Harder tests do not measure every needed strength.
Fact 8 says these skills are learnable. Temperament matters, but it does not freeze the person's next practiced response.
Fact 9 does not set IQ against emotion. It asks whether arousal guides attention well or narrows judgment too much.
Fact 1 supports cue perception first. The common error is treating empathy as thought guessing.
Fact 2 says emotion often appears in nonverbal signals before clear speech. Words alone are not enough.
Fact 3 supports shared inner states through attunement. The near miss is seeing attunement as spoiling or erasing distress.
Fact 4 says chronic mismatch can blunt trust in feelings. Ignored feelings do not simply disappear.
Fact 5 requires self-awareness. Empathy fails when your feeling merges with another person's signal.
Fact 6 ties social ease to fewer emotional misreads. It is not pure personality.
Fact 7 says distress can block empathy when it overwhelms attention. More distress is not always more care.
Fact 8 supports pain registering as significant. The error is reducing morality to rules alone or replacing rules entirely.
Fact 9 says accuracy can improve through attention to cues. The wrong move is treating cue reading as fixed.
Fact 1 supports reading the other person's display while regulating your own. Talking more is the common error, not the first move.
Fact 2 says one person's mood can shape a group's atmosphere. The near misses keep mood private until words or tasks take over.
Fact 3 supports reading the setting along with the face. The distractors either flatten all expressions or dismiss expression entirely.
Fact 4 says poor nonverbal reading can lead to rejection without hostile intent. The wrong choices turn rejection into meanness or passivity.
Fact 5 names timing, turn-taking, and synchrony. Good motives and clear opinions do not replace the timing of the exchange.
Fact 6 supports leadership as tone-setting in a small group. The other choices treat title as the starting point.
Fact 7 supports fast noticing after a misstep. Ignoring the frozen smile or explaining intent first can miss the needed repair.
Fact 8 says charm without empathy becomes manipulation. Reading a room can be used to steer, not necessarily to care.
Fact 9 says the social arts translate inner regulation into public behavior. Private calm alone is the common error.
Fact 1 supports repetition as training. The near miss waits for age to solve what the family is already practicing each time.
Fact 2 says authoritative parenting combines warmth with firm boundaries. Warmth is not the loss of a rule or a reward after compliance.
Fact 3 names the risk: dismissal teaches avoidance, not regulation. The other choices describe permissive rule loss or repair practice.
Fact 4 supports noticing and naming first. Naming is not a reward for drama; it makes the feeling easier to guide.
Fact 5 separates feeling from action. Anger can be accepted while the slammed door still gets a limit and repair.
Fact 6 says conflict teaches scripts. The goal is not zero conflict; it is a visible way to disagree and repair.
Fact 7 warns that harsh criticism can move inward. It may motivate in the moment while teaching shame as self-talk.
Fact 8 ties secure coaching to empathy and impulse control. The near misses split discipline from feeling or hide feeling entirely.
Fact 9 makes family the early training ground. School matters, but it is not the first place children rehearse emotional responses.
Fact 1 says trauma may return through bodily alarm, not just ordinary recall. A cleaner timeline can matter later, but it does not explain the first surge.
Fact 2 links reminders to distress because emotional memory ties cues to danger. Treating the trigger as a chosen reaction misreads the timing.
Fact 3 supports both sides: avoidance protects short-term calm and keeps the fear network untested. The tempting error treats relief as a cure.
Fact 4 says recovery begins with reliable safety. Insight and mourning may matter, but Herman's order keeps them after safety.
Fact 5 says talking through trauma too soon can overwhelm. The near miss assumes any careful listener can make timing irrelevant.
Fact 6 supports gradual exposure because the brain learns reminders can be survived. Flooding and total avoidance both miss the learning window.
Fact 7 says children need adult containment. Assuming they forget quickly can leave them alone with alarms they cannot yet manage.
Fact 8 frames symptoms as adaptations to danger that persist after danger ends. Weakness language turns a survival response into blame.
Fact 9 says emotional relearning changes response strength even when memory remains. Erasing or replacing memory is the common wrong promise.
Fact 1 says emotional illiteracy appears in patterns of aggression, despair, and risk. The isolated-choice reading misses shared gaps in impulse, distress, and response.
Fact 2 treats adolescent risk indicators as public evidence of unmet needs. The numbers do not replace context, but they are not irrelevant to emotion.
Fact 3 links impulse problems to violence when conflict skills are absent. This does not erase harm; it shows what a consequence must also teach.
Fact 4 says depression risk rises when children lack tools for interpreting and managing distress. The key is not a quick fix, but a missing skill set.
Fact 5 says substance use can function as attempted mood regulation. Rule-breaking may still matter, but the emotional function cannot be dismissed.
Fact 6 says eating disorders can involve emotional control through body control. The vanity reading is too shallow and misses the need to notice signals early.
Fact 7 ties isolation to trouble reading and repairing interactions. Some solitude is fine, but broken repair can make distance grow.
Fact 8 says prevention must begin before crisis behaviors harden. Waiting makes the old response easier to repeat and harder to unlearn.
Fact 9 makes emotional literacy a civic and public-health concern. It belongs in public prevention because arousal and judgment shape risk in shared life.
Fact 1 says emotional literacy is taught through repeated classroom practice. The near misses assume children learn emotion without instruction.
Fact 2 supports vocabulary as a tool for self-control. Calling it decoration misses how a name changes what the child can do next.
Fact 3 says conflict lessons work best when tied to real peer incidents. A purely invented case can dodge the practiced response children need.
Fact 4 says teachers model regulation by how they handle disruption. The other choices treat adult emotion as irrelevant to the lesson.
Fact 5 names self-awareness and self-management as explicit competencies. SEL is not only self-esteem or only outward behavior.
Fact 6 supports social awareness and relationship skills as teachable domains. The near misses make them fixed or less central.
Fact 7 links responsible decision-making to emotion, consequences, and values. The other choices split emotion from judgment.
Fact 8 says whole-school consistency helps practice become habit. One lesson can name a skill without making it durable.
Fact 9 connects prevention and character formation through practiced skill. The near misses separate them or replace practice with speeches.
Fact 1 supports the 2017 overlap. A 1965 visual split should not be reused as if it still described most people.
Fact 2 says both moved from roughly 240 to 250 deaths per 1,000 to below 35, with Saudi Arabia moving faster.
Fact 3 points to the majority before the extremes. The poorest and richest groups are real, but they do not define normal global life.
Fact 4 supports the ladder because it shows middle positions. The common error is treating four levels as a softer binary.
Fact 5 points to lag. The World Bank wording mattered because an institution can preserve an old category after the distribution changes.
Fact 6 separates the measures. The global extreme-poverty line sits far below many rich-country relative poverty thresholds.
Fact 7 says the data stay the same while the frame changes. Survival wording can reduce misreading without changing the facts.
Fact 8 warns that people inside one country can live on different levels. Averages are useful, but they can compress internal differences.
Fact 9 says the cure is distributions, not positivity. This method keeps severe poverty visible while rejecting a false empty gap.
Fact 1 says the child population is projected to be about the same in 2100 as in 2017 after a mid-century peak. The other choices turn total growth into the wrong child story.
Fact 2 points to age-structure momentum. More people surviving into adulthood and old age can lift total population even when births per woman fall.
Fact 3 gives the 1950 and 2017 averages and supports a major decline. The other choices keep the common error that family size barely changed.
Fact 4 names several determinants working together. The common error is turning a fertility transition into a one-cause story about contraception alone.
Fact 5 says a small part of a curve can look straight. The first check is the viewing window, not the neatness or drama of the recent segment.
Fact 6 supports a gallery of shapes. Saturation, thresholds, and behavior change can bend a line, so income alone does not make every indicator straight.
Fact 7 says UN forecasts have a measurable record. That does not make them perfect, but it does make them more than unchecked guesses.
Fact 8 says replacement depends on mortality conditions and cites about 2.3 globally. The simple two-parent arithmetic misses deaths before replacement can happen.
Fact 9 gives the core repair: ask why the line might bend before extrapolating. A recent slope without a mechanism is only a drawing habit.
Fact 1 separates reported fear from mortality risk. Snakes, heights, and public speaking can rank high in fear without ranking high as causes of death.
Fact 2 supports the large raw decline. The later count is still tragic, but it is far lower than the early-century average.
Fact 3 says per-capita risk fell even more. The raw count matters, but deaths per million adjusts for the larger exposed population.
Fact 4 names the earthquake, tsunami, and evacuation harms. The cited official accounts reported no confirmed direct deaths from the leak itself.
Fact 6 requires exposure. Fatalities mean little for safety judgment unless they are compared with passenger miles and flight volume.
Fact 8 separates media attention from death risk. Terrorism can be salient because intent and drama are newsworthy, not because airtime measures mortality burden.
Fact 9 says risk combines danger, exposure, and probability rather than emotional intensity. Scale decides whether it deserves scarce resources.
Fact 7 keeps psychosocial effects and evacuation damage in view. The source does not limit harm to confirmed radiation deaths.
Fact 5 says uncertainty should widen ranges, not end comparison. A cautious range is better than pretending the data are useless or clean.
Fact 1 says the Nacala deaths needed births, population, and hospital records before they could guide action. The raw count alone can misdirect scarce help.
Fact 3 supports ranking by lives saved per dollar in poor settings. Advanced care may matter, but it is not always the best first use of scarce funds.
Fact 4 says people overestimate visible proportions. The UK guesses of 25 versus 13 percent and 59 versus 23 percent show salience inflating shares.
Fact 8 says the denominator must fit the decision: per birth, per dollar, per population, or per exposure. A bad denominator can mislead too.
Fact 5 says infant death totals need births and trends. A large total can coexist with a falling rate, so risk per child matters.
Fact 2 says Mozambique's poverty and extremely low doctor density made prioritization severe. Scarcity raises the opportunity cost of each intervention.
Fact 7 says rare dramatic attacks can receive more attention than repeated intimate-partner killings. Policy focus should track frequency and preventability.
Fact 9 gives the repair: compare and divide. The number may be useful, but not until it is placed against a relevant whole or alternative.
Fact 6 says war totals need denominators and context. A remembered number can be emotionally large without being the largest current priority.
Fact 1 says household objects can resemble each other across China and Nigeria at similar income levels. Country-first guessing misses that pattern.
Fact 2 makes Africa too varied for one mental category. The distance comparison is a warning against treating the continent as one close, uniform place.
Fact 3 links diabetes care costs to fragile budgets. The rich-country shortcut fails when insulin and care consume money a household cannot spare.
Fact 4 says met and unmet need must be separated. Use alone can hide women who want to avoid pregnancy but lack contraception.
Fact 5 rejects origin as the safety test. Toxicity depends on compound and dose, so natural and synthetic are not enough.
Fact 6 does not make expertise worthless. It says broad medical rules need evidence and revision when later feedback shows harm.
Fact 7 treats the Salhi material as concrete household evidence. One home can sharpen observation, but it cannot define a country.
Fact 8 uses distance to expose category absurdity. A shared continent label can hide how far apart and varied the cases are.
Fact 9 says the cure is not category refusal. Split, merge, or replace the label when it no longer predicts the case at hand.
Fact 1 says several North African countries reached life expectancy above the world average and near historical Sweden. The lesson is movement, not sameness.
Fact 2 says Iran's lower 2017 rate undercuts religious destiny stories. The rate points to social and policy change, not a fixed label.
Fact 5 says FSA photographs and Dirt Sweden documented hardship in countries later seen as rich. Comfort can be recent, not timeless.
Fact 9 says the cure for destiny thinking is noticing slow change. Gradual movement can matter long before it becomes headline-sized.
Fact 6 is the guardrail. The source rejects fixed destiny, but it also rejects automatic catch-up when war or weak institutions block change.
Fact 7 says religious categories do not determine family size. Conditions such as income, education, and health can cut across labels.
Fact 4 says several infrastructure indicators improved over decades. Low levels still matter, but they do not erase movement.
Fact 8 says forecasts should be checked against their record. The right move is neither obedience nor dismissal, but review.
Fact 3 links fertility decline with gains in women's schooling and life expectancy. The transition was broader than one rate.
Fact 1 supports scoping expertise. The Lindau miss is not a reason to mock experts or erase facts; it shows that skill in one field does not cover all global knowledge.
Fact 2 points to broad access. A disease campaign can help, but Alma Ata warns that campaigns do not replace clinics, staff, trust, and local reach.
Fact 3 says schooling is not only curriculum. Energy, light, and connectivity can change learning conditions, so the second tool looks beyond the classroom plan.
Fact 4 supports the outcome check. More spending across categories can sit beside no matching life-expectancy gain, so cost alone is not quality.
Fact 5 does not reject democracy. It says elections are not a guaranteed repair when violence and weak institutions change how the tool works.
Fact 6 says markets can help without being complete. The better memo keeps the tool and adds the systems that let growth reach people.
Fact 7 favors humble updating over confidence. Curiosity and revision improve forecasts; one-lens certainty can sound strong while seeing less.
Fact 8 says ownership slogans are too thin. Shared resources need rules, incentives, and local management that change extraction behavior.
Fact 9 says the work is matching tools to mechanisms. A second measure and an outcome test beat the hunt for one theory that explains everything.
Fact 1 supports looking for the repeated mechanism. Blaming the latest worker may feel precise, but the loop can keep producing the miss.
Fact 2 points to institutional work. Generosity can help, but the source case turns on procurement, tender design, and supply discipline.
Fact 6 grounds the answer in Monrovia contact tracing. The near-miss is hero worship, whether the hero is foreign or only symbolic.
Fact 9 separates responsibility from causal diagnosis. The blame check delays accusation to find a changeable cause; it does not erase accountability.
Fact 3 says distorted coverage can be sincere. Dishonesty is one possibility, but shared skewed knowledge and attention markets can also mislead.
Fact 4 points to legal incentives around carriers and smuggling. The trap is treating boat travel as a simple personal preference.
This stem asks for the mistake. Fact 7 rejects single-leader explanations because fertility had already fallen before the famous policy.
Fact 8 makes institutions practical. Records, services, and enforcement show capacity; a label or logo can leave the work invisible.
Fact 5 uses the Danish rescue to separate the physical act from its legal and moral context. A boat can mean different things in different systems.
Fact 1 says controls can fail when contacts move by canoe or forest path. Visibility is not enough, and the answer is not slow review; it is checking the route.
Fact 2 warns that urgency creates false binaries. The policy analyst should keep ranges and options alive, not force one line or treat uncertainty as denial.
Fact 5 says data freshness differs by indicator. GDP and CO2 can have very different lags, so the analyst needs dates per measure, not one shared clock.
Fact 4 says repetition can amplify weak original estimates. The issue is source-chain strength, not the number's fame or a reason to ignore migration.
Fact 3 separates serious climate risk from one simple event. Rejecting a single catastrophe frame is not denial; it protects a complex risk from a bad story.
Fact 6 places global pandemic on the short risk list. Factfulness narrows attention to major risks; it does not erase pandemic concern.
Fact 7 says overuse is dangerous, but underaccess can also kill. Careful action must see both harms instead of turning panic into a blanket rule.
Fact 8 says extreme poverty remains an ongoing risk. A falling rate does not erase the harder remaining cases or justify headline-driven attention.
Fact 9 supports disciplined speed: small checks keep facts in the loop. It rejects both blind sharing and waiting for perfect certainty.
Fact 1 points to reusable Gapminder materials and a teacher community. The practice is repeated correction, not one clean reveal or one private reading.
Fact 2 says services and industries shift across income levels. The stale move is West selling to Rest, even when it adds more examples.
Fact 3 says development changes supply chains. The error is treating a low-income production location as fixed after it appears on the map.
Fact 4 frames Ghana, Nigeria, and Kenya as investment opportunities. The aid-only frame is the common error, not the business lens.
Fact 5 says the Atlas maps existing industries and skills into plausible next capabilities. It guides choices; it does not bless ambition afterward.
Fact 6 says constructive journalism improves information quality. The near miss is thinking context means ignoring or replacing bad events.
Fact 7 says local data can reveal local misconceptions. The error is assuming only global facts need correction or that nearness makes knowledge easy.
Fact 9 says factfulness is maintenance. A corrected chart can go stale; waiting for a major error lets the old story rebuild.
Fact 1 supports reusable classroom materials, and the mechanism is practice with feedback. A lecture may inform, but it does not by itself rehearse correction.
Fact 1 names skewed payoff as the central concept. The mechanism asks for win and loss size, not only the visible count.
Fact 2 says high-probability small gains can be inferior depending on payoff size. The key keeps both sides in view.
Fact 3 separates win rate from expected value. Magnitude can dominate frequency when the wrong occasion is large enough.
Fact 4 uses option selling to make the payoff shape concrete. It does not say every option sale is automatically bad.
Fact 5 says option buyers may look foolish most days while retaining rare upside. It still requires the payoff to justify the cost.
Fact 6 says skewness makes averages hard to infer from short samples. The tail may not have appeared yet.
Fact 7 states this directly. A strategy can be right often and still lose if the wrong occasions are large enough.
Fact 8 says risk communication fails when it gives probability without consequence. The amount at stake completes the sentence.
Fact 9 warns against glorifying rare upside while ignoring cost. Skewness asks for payoff shape, not romance about tails.
Fact 1 makes probability blindness the central concept. It explains why emotional conviction can split from mathematical exposure.
Fact 2 says visible results can diverge from process quality. The desk is judging the path it sees, not the distribution it does not see.
Fact 3 warns that reward can arrive before the relevant adverse state. Concrete wins do not make abstract exposure safe.
Fact 4 names availability: vivid events feel more likely than dull statistical risks. The story is salient, not necessarily more probable.
Fact 5 says pattern detection overfires in random data. Hidden alternatives can change what observed success means.
Fact 6 says gains and losses do not track expected value cleanly. Reputation often sees the outcome before it sees the distribution.
Fact 7 says training helps but does not remove the pull of outcomes. A clean story after the fact can be fitted to chance.
Fact 8 says a person can understand randomness and still feel fooled. The check asks how much is at risk, how much evidence supports it, and what the bad case costs.
Fact 9 corrects the shallow lesson. Probability blindness is not an insult to intelligence; it calls for compensation around intuition.
Fact 1 names practical skepticism as the center. Carneades is the entry point, but the working idea is graded belief that resists false certainty.
Fact 2 says responsible action refuses to confuse plausible with certain. One result can hide alternatives and the cost of being wrong.
Fact 3 ties Carneades to challenges against certain knowledge. The common error is reading repeated reward or force as safety.
Fact 4 supports probabilistic belief over binary certainty in uncertain domains. The honest move is grading confidence, not flattening it.
Fact 5 says skepticism protects against early closure. A coherent story can be fitted after chance has already selected the visible path.
Fact 6 says practical life still requires action, so doubt needs decision rules. Reputation can reflect lucky timing and selective observation.
Fact 7 links Sextus and Pyrrhonian tools to suspending overconfident judgment. Neat stories can be built after the outcome is known.
Fact 8 says markets punish certainty. Risk judgment should start with position size, the record behind it, and the loss branch, not emotional vividness.
Fact 9 warns against the easy misreading that skepticism refuses commitments. The sharper version grades belief and acts without fake certainty.
Fact 1 says the problem remains when people want to save more later than now. The bare menu answer misses the timing and payroll friction.
Fact 2 says defaults work by changing the path of least resistance. Direct persuasion and full reading are not the only routes to behavior.
Fact 3 treats Skylar's delay as an active savings setting. While she waits, some default remains in force and shapes the outcome.
Fact 4 favors clearer mapping, not more paper by itself. The raise link helps workers compare today's choice with later welfare.
Fact 5 says opt-out freedom matters only when refusal is practical. Higher saving or hidden disclosure cannot carry the liberty claim alone.
Fact 6 names Richard Thaler as a real-world anchor with observable design features. A generic or invented story is weaker grounding.
Fact 7 says Brigitte Madrian supplies a second anchor, reducing one-story overfit. It does not erase the earlier case or make every menu identical.
Fact 8 draws the line between chooser welfare and designer preference. Clarity and measurement do not justify improving the designer's favorite result.
Fact 9 says Save More Tomorrow fits the nudge frame because the preferred arrangement remains avoidable. A mandate carries heavier penalties or removes alternatives.
Fact 1 says portfolio choice overload remains even with formal choice. A long menu can push crude splitting or delay when the architecture is poor.
Fact 2 supports Wendy. Defaults, salience, and friction can change behavior without a speech, especially when the choice is hard.
Fact 3 treats Phoebe's pause as consequential. A default, status quo, or old allocation can keep acting while fees still matter.
Fact 4 favors clearer mapping at the decision point. More documents can fail if the saver cannot use them while choosing.
Fact 5 says steering needs a practical opt-out. A hidden form is not enough, even when the target-date path may help many savers.
Fact 7 names the U.S. SEC as an independent anchor. A real design case carries more weight than an invented or isolated story.
Fact 8 asks whether the portfolio path serves the saver rather than Claude's taste. Better design is justified by likely saver welfare, not a designer favorite.
Fact 9 says the nudge frame depends on an avoidable preferred path. A mandate removes or heavily penalizes alternatives.
Fact 1 points to overload and crude diversification rules. Equal splitting may reveal an unusable menu, not a well-formed preference.
Fact 1 says retirement menu design remains a problem when options are hard to use. A formal list alone can still overwhelm or mislead.
Fact 2 says defaults, salience, and friction can influence behavior without argument. The path of least resistance matters.
Fact 3 makes Blake's non-click a live outcome. Delay can leave an implicit result in force, even when the chooser feels undecided.
Fact 4 favors clearer mapping through low-cost diversification. More documents do not help if the saver cannot use them at the choice point.
Fact 5 says opt-out protects freedom only when exit is practical. Better averages or hidden disclosure cannot carry the whole defense.
Fact 6 names Sweden as a real-world anchor with observable design features. A hypothetical or shopping scene weakens the factual grounding.
Fact 7 says 401(k) automatic enrollment supplies a second anchor for the same design problem. It does not erase Sweden or prove all plans identical.
Fact 8 separates the chooser's welfare from designer preference. The point is not the agency's favorite metric or a paper-only exit.
Fact 9 marks retirement nudges by the exit they preserve. The preset path may steer, but it must stay avoidable; mandates close or punish other routes.
Fact 1 says the problem is Medicare choice overload. Formal options can still be unusable when complexity makes good matching hard.
Fact 2 says plan matching changes the path of least resistance. A nudge can work through defaults, salience, and friction.
Fact 3 warns Yvonne that no click is still a path. An old plan or implicit default can keep operating while she waits.
Fact 4 says review improves choice by mapping options to later welfare. More documents alone can fail at the decision point.
Fact 5 says intelligent assignment protects freedom only when exit is realistic. A costly refusal changes the design's character.
Fact 6 says Part D grounds the claim with named institutions and observable design features. A bare hypothetical is weaker evidence.
Fact 7 says Plan Finder supplies an independent anchor. The same mechanism appears outside one isolated case.
Fact 8 puts Ella's question first: does the match help the enrollee? Office convenience cannot stand in for chooser welfare.
Fact 9 says the preferred arrangement remains avoidable in the nudge framework. A mandate makes alternatives much costlier.
Fact 1 says formal options are not enough when the architecture makes a choice hard to use. The bare-options view misses how the registry path works.
Fact 2 says friction and defaults can steer without direct persuasion. Marc's speech-only view ignores the force of the easiest route.
Fact 3 says delay is not neutral. While the driver waits, some default or status quo still governs the record.
Fact 4 favors usable mapping over more paper. The prompt connects today's answer to the later registry outcome at the moment of choice.
Fact 5 says freedom depends on a realistic opt-out. Better outcomes do not justify a refusal path that ordinary people cannot use.
Fact 6 makes Eric Johnson a grounding anchor, not a shortcut to one universal rule. The value is that the design features can be checked.
Fact 7 says the license registry is an independent anchor. It reduces overfit to one case without replacing the other levers.
Fact 8 asks whose interests the donor rule serves. A higher count matters, but it cannot replace the driver's or family's welfare standard.
Fact 9 draws the organ-donor boundary around practical exit. Donation may be favored, but a nudge differs from a mandate while leaving remains easy.
Fact 1 says formal options are not enough. Environmental harms are distant and invisible, so the setup needs feedback and social comparison.
Fact 2 supports Adele. Feedback, salience, defaults, and friction can shape the easy route without a persuasive essay.
Fact 3 makes Kira's postponed comparison consequential. Waiting can leave a default or status quo active while the hard comparison stays unseen.
Fact 4 favors clearer mapping at the decision point. More documents can fail when readers cannot use them during the choice.
